findings.who: A filer born in 1965 or 1966 who took a Roth IRA distribution after turning 59½ in 2025. The custodian coded it J in box 7 instead of Q or T, and the distribution includes taxable earnings, for example because the 5-year period is not met.
findings.why_no: The computed gate only recognizes code 1 or code S (a SIMPLE IRA within 2 years) as an early distribution. Code J makes the gate false, so the age question is never asked and the line is set to false.
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2, exception 12: "Distributions incorrectly indicated as early distributions by code 1, J, or S in box 7 of Form 1099-R. Include on line 2 the amount you received when you were age 59 1/2 or older."
findings.fix: Add code J to the early-distribution helper for this gate, so it reads code 1, J, or S, and ask the same age question for a Roth distribution coded J.

findings.who: A filer whose plan dated a check before their 59½ date, but who received it on or after that date, for example a check mailed in late December that arrived after the filer turned 59½.
findings.why_no: The question asks about age on "the date of every payment." The filer reads that as the payer's issue date and answers No, while the IRS text measures the amount "you received when you were age 59 1/2 or older."
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2, exception 12: "Include on line 2 the amount you received when you were age 59 1/2 or older."
findings.fix: Reword the question as "Were you age 59½ or older on the date you received every payment of this money?" and match the help text.

findings.who: A filer born in 1964 or earlier, clearly over 59½ for all of 2025, whose distribution was coded 1 in error. The computed gate is false because the birth year settles the age.
findings.why_no: The gate excludes this filer because their age is settled. Unless another line treats a settled age of 59½ or older as exception 12, the miscoded amount gets no exclusion.
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2, exception 12: "Distributions incorrectly indicated as early distributions by code 1, J, or S in box 7 of Form 1099-R."
findings.fix: Confirm that a separate computed path applies exception 12 automatically when the birth year shows 59½ or older at every payment in 2025 (born before 1965 with code 1, J, or S). If no such path exists, add one.

locators: p. 5, Line 2, exception 12, "Distributions incorrectly indicated as early distributions by code 1, J, or S in box 7 of Form 1099-R. Include on line 2 the amount you received when you were age 59 1/2 or older."

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly enters the spouse's Form 1099-R. The spouse was born in 1934 and took a total distribution from a former employer's qualified plan. The filer at the keyboard was born in 1942.
findings.why_no: The gate's parenthetical, '(you, or the person you inherited it from)', names only 'you' and an inheritance. The filer answers with their own 1942 birth date. Unlike the gated question, the gate never says 'or your spouse on a joint return'.
findings.line: retirement.lump_sum_if_born_before_averaging_date (the Yes that ends the interview, and so the refusal, is never reached)
findings.irs_text: "If you or the plan participant was born before January 2, 1936, you could pay less tax on the distribution. See Form 4972." (i1040gi 2025, p. 30, Lump-Sum Distributions)
findings.fix: Word the gate per document and person: 'Was the plan participant who earned this balance (you, your spouse on a joint return, or the person you inherited it from) born before January 2, 1936?' Better, ask for the participant's birth date and compute the condition.

findings.who: A former spouse born in 1948 receives, under a qualified domestic relations order, a distribution of the entire share of an ex-husband's qualified plan balance. The ex-husband, the plan participant, was born in 1934 and is still living.
findings.why_no: The parenthetical lists only 'you, or the person you inherited it from'. The alternate payee did not earn the balance and did not inherit it, so they read the list as complete and answer for themselves (born 1948).
findings.line: retirement.lump_sum_if_born_before_averaging_date (the out-of-scope Form 4972 case and its refusal are missed)
findings.irs_text: "If you or the plan participant was born before January 2, 1936, you could pay less tax on the distribution. See Form 4972." (i1040gi 2025, p. 30); see also "distributions under qualified domestic relations orders" (p. 30, Rollovers)
findings.fix: Name the plan participant directly and add the alternate-payee case: '…(you, your spouse, a former spouse whose plan paid you under a court order (QDRO), or the person you inherited it from)'.

findings.who: A successor beneficiary (born 1975) receives the whole remaining plan balance. They inherited the balance from their mother (born 1950), who had inherited it from the original participant, a grandfather born in 1933.
findings.why_no: 'The person you inherited it from' is the mother, born 1950, so the filer answers no. The instructions key the rule to the plan participant.
findings.irs_text: "If you or the plan participant was born before January 2, 1936…" (i1040gi 2025, p. 30)
findings.fix: Say 'the plan participant (the employee who originally earned the balance)' instead of 'the person you inherited it from'.

locators: pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

findings.who: A beneficiary receiving a survivor annuity from a deceased employee who died before August 21, 1996, where neither the employee nor the beneficiary made after-tax contributions. The beneficiary is entitled to the death benefit exclusion of up to $5,000.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only whether money 'paid into' the plan was 'already taxed when it went in', and boxes 5 and 9b are blank. Nothing taxed went in, so No is the truthful answer, yet the exclusion counts as cost for the Simplified Method.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 29, Simplified Method Worksheet: 'If you are the beneficiary of a deceased employee or former employee who died before August 21, 1996, include any death benefit exclusion that you are entitled to (up to $5,000) in the amount entered on line 2 below.'
findings.fix: Add a gate branch: 'Are you receiving this as the survivor or beneficiary of an employee who died before August 21, 1996?' A yes should open the Simplified Method questions with the death benefit exclusion as cost.

findings.who: A plan participant whose plan basis did not come from after-tax contributions at the time of deposit. Examples are a participant taxed in an earlier year on a deemed distribution from a defaulted plan loan, or one taxed each year on employer-paid life insurance costs inside the plan. Another is an employee taxed on employer contributions in a year the plan was not qualified.
findings.why_no: The words 'already taxed when it went in' and 'after-tax contributions' describe the filer's own contributions taxed at deposit. These amounts were taxed later, or were employer money, and the payer often leaves box 9b blank.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30, Cost: 'Your cost is generally your net investment in the plan as of the annuity starting date. It doesn't include pre-tax contributions.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Do you (or the person you inherited from) have any amount in this plan that was already taxed to you, whether when it went in or later? This includes after-tax contributions, employer contributions or insurance costs you paid tax on, or a defaulted plan loan reported as income.' Use box 5 or 9b as examples of yes, not as the test.

findings.who: A retiree who made after-tax contributions to a pension plan or a 401(k), shown in the retiree's own records or plan statements. The payer left boxes 5 and 9b blank and checked 'taxable amount not determined', as many payers do.
findings.why_no: The help says 'An amount in box 5 or box 9b means yes.' A filer reads the blank boxes as meaning no, even though the gated Simplified Method question itself refers to 'box 9b or your records'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30, Cost: 'Your net investment may be shown in box 9b of Form 1099-R.' i1040gi p. 28: 'If your Form 1099-R doesn't show the taxable amount, you must use the General Rule ... to figure the taxable part.'
findings.fix: Change the help to: 'An amount in box 5 or 9b means yes, but blank boxes do not mean no; also check your plan statements or records for after-tax contributions.'

findings.who: A retired state or local government employee, such as a teacher or police officer, or a federal CSRS or FERS retiree, whose mandatory pension contributions were withheld from salary after tax. This applies, for example, before a 414(h) pickup took effect.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of payroll-withheld retirement contributions as pre-tax, like a 401(k) deferral. They answer 'not already taxed', especially with box 9b blank.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 28, Partially Taxable Pensions and Annuities: 'If your Form 1099-R doesn't show the taxable amount, you must use the General Rule ... But if your annuity starting date ... was after July 1, 1986, see Simplified Method.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Mandatory contributions withheld from your pay for a government or employer pension were often after-tax (for example, federal CSRS/FERS contributions, or state plan contributions before your employer picked them up). Check your plan statement.'

findings.who: A federal civil service retiree who chose the alternative annuity option and received a lump-sum refund of their own contributions at retirement. Monthly payments followed.
findings.why_no: The retiree reasons that their taxed contributions were paid back in the lump sum, so none of the money now in the pension was 'already taxed'. Answering No suppresses the CSRS alternative-annuity question and the refusal it leads to.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30, Caution: 'If you received U.S. Civil Service retirement benefits and you chose the alternative annuity option, see Pub. 721 to figure the taxable part of your annuity. Do not use the Simplified Method Worksheet in these instructions.'
findings.fix: Ask the CSRS alternative-annuity question for any civil service (OPM, CSA 1099-R) pension, regardless of the cost gate. Or add 'including contributions later refunded to you in a lump sum' to the gate.

findings.who: A filer who bought a nonqualified annuity from an insurance company with their own money and now receives periodic payments reported on Form 1099-R. Box 9b is blank and the insurer reported the investment as premiums, not contributions.
findings.why_no: The gate speaks of a 'pension or annuity' and 'after-tax contributions'. A buyer who paid premiums for a contract does not think of them as contributions 'paid into' a pension. Answering No suppresses the own-annuity question and its refusal.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30, Simplified Method condition 2a: 'The payments are from a qualified employee plan, a qualified employee annuity, or a tax-sheltered annuity.' i1040gi p. 28: 'you must use the General Rule explained in Pub. 939 to figure the taxable part.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Is this an annuity you bought yourself from an insurance company?' before or independently of the cost gate. Or add to the gate: 'premiums you paid for an annuity you bought yourself count as yes.'

findings.who: A surviving spouse or beneficiary receiving payments under a joint and survivor annuity, where the deceased retiree made the after-tax contributions. The survivor's Form 1099-R shows no box 9b amount.
findings.why_no: The survivor paid nothing into the plan personally and reads 'the money paid into this pension' as their own payments. They answer No, losing the retiree's fixed tax-free amount and the questions about start date and age that refer to the retiree.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 34, Survivors of retirees: 'If the retiree was reporting the annuity under the Simplified Method, the part of each payment that is tax free is the same as the tax-free amount figured by the retiree at the annuity starting date.'
findings.fix: Reword the gate: 'Did you, or the retiree or employee you receive this from as a survivor or beneficiary, pay any already-taxed money into this pension or annuity?'

locators: p. 30, Simplified Method, conditions 1 and 2; p. 28, Partially Taxable Pensions and Annuities; , Distribution On or After Annuity Starting Date, "If you receive a nonperiodic payment from your annuity contract on or after the annuity starting date, you must generally include all of the payment in gross income."; , Survivors of retirees, "If the retiree was reporting the annuity under the Simplified Method, the part of each payment that is tax free is the same as the tax-free amount figured by the retiree at the annuity starting date"
pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

used.how: pages named by another document's citation

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse, not the filer, receives a disability pension from the spouse's former employer's plan. The spouse is 48, and the plan's minimum retirement age is 55.
findings.why_no: The gate and its parent helper say "paid to you because you became disabled" and "were you younger" with no "or your spouse". Only the gated question says "For this person (you, or your spouse on a joint return)". The filer is past 55, or was never disabled, so they truthfully answer about themselves and say no.
findings.line: retirement.dis_all_early_if_early (and with it the move of the pension from lines 5a/5b to line 1h)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 28: "Don't include the following payments on lines 5a and 5b. Instead, report them on line 1h. • Disability pensions received before you reach the minimum retirement age set by your employer."
findings.fix: Name the recipient in the gate and its parent helper: "Was any of this paid to the person this Form 1099-R is for (you, or your spouse on a joint return) because they became disabled..." and "was that person younger than...".

findings.who: A disabled firefighter aged 40 whose plan allows unreduced retirement after 20 years of service at any age. A FERS employee aged 57, past the FERS 'Minimum Retirement Age' of 57, who has only 8 years of service, so the plan would not yet have let them retire without the disability.
findings.why_no: The parenthetical "(its minimum retirement age)" names a plan term. For the FERS employee, the plan's published MRA is 57 and they have reached it, so they answer no. For the 20-and-out firefighter, there is no stated age, so they answer no or treat the question as not applying. In both cases the person was younger than the age at which they could first have retired without the disability.
findings.line: retirement.dis_all_early_if_early (disability pension then reported as a pension on lines 5a/5b instead of wages on line 1h)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25: "Disability pensions shown on Form 1099-R if you haven't reached the minimum retirement age set by your employer" are reported on line 1h; "Disability pensions received after you reach minimum retirement age ... are reported on lines 5a and 5b."
findings.fix: Ask about facts the filer can check: "When each payment was made, could you already have retired under this plan (with a pension, reduced or not) if you had not become disabled, given your age and years of service?" Add help saying that a plan term called 'minimum retirement age' (such as the FERS MRA) does not decide the answer if service requirements were not yet met.

findings.who: A retired police officer under the plan's minimum retirement age whose governmental plan pays part of the disability pension straight to a health insurer as premiums under the public safety officer election.
findings.why_no: The parent helper asks whether any of this was "paid to you" because you became disabled. The filer may count only the checks they received, and treat the premium amounts paid directly to the insurer as not "paid to you". If all of it went to the insurer, they answer no.
findings.line: retirement.dis_all_early_if_early (the line 1h treatment and the 'PSO' notation next to line 1h)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi pp. 28-30: "The distribution can be made directly from the plan to the provider... If you are retired on disability and reporting your disability pension on line 1h, include only the taxable amount on that line and enter "PSO" and the amount excluded on the line next to line 1h."
findings.fix: Change "paid to you" to "paid to you or for you (including amounts the plan sent directly to an insurer)".

locators: p. 25, "Disability pensions received after you reach minimum retirement age and other payments shown on Form 1099-R (other than payments from an IRA) are reported on lines 5a and 5b"

p. 25, "Disability pensions shown on Form 1099-R if you haven’t reached the minimum retirement age set by your employer", "Disability pensions received after you reach minimum retirement age and other payments shown on Form 1099-R (other than payments from an IRA) are reported on lines 5a and 5b"
pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

findings.who: A military retiree whose Form 1099-R retired pay was granted for years of service. The VA later awarded a disability rating, possibly retroactive, or the retiree has combat-related disability retired pay that is partly excludable.
findings.why_no: The pay was granted for length of service, not 'because you became disabled'. So the retiree truthfully answers no to the parent gate and never sees 'Is it a disability pension for service in the armed forces?'
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 28: 'Fully taxable pensions and annuities also include military retirement pay shown on Form 1099-R. For details on military disability pensions, see Pub. 525.'
findings.fix: Ask the military question for every pension, outside the disability gate: 'Is any of this military retired pay (for you or your spouse), or has the VA given either of you a disability rating that covers any period of this pay?' Refuse on yes.

findings.who: A worker who stopped working because of a disability and receives monthly payments from the employer's pension plan. The worker does not know whether the plan formally 'provides for disability retirement'. The Form 1099-R shows code 3 (disability) in box 7.
findings.why_no: The phrase 'under a plan that provides for disability retirement' is a legal classification of the plan document. A filer who cannot confirm it answers no, or treats the payment as an ordinary early pension.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 28: 'Don't include the following payments on lines 5a and 5b. Instead, report them on line 1h. • Disability pensions received before you reach the minimum retirement age set by your employer.'
findings.fix: Gate on facts the filer can check: 'Does box 7 of this Form 1099-R show code 3, or were any of these payments made because you or your spouse became disabled?' On yes, ask about the plan's disability provision and the minimum retirement age, with help text that names the plan administrator.

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse receives a disability pension, possibly before the plan's minimum retirement age, or one resulting from a terrorist attack. The filer answers the questions for the whole return.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'paid to you because you became disabled' and does not mention a spouse. The gated questions do say 'For this person (you, or your spouse on a joint return)'. The filer answers no for themselves.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 28: 'Disability pensions received before you reach the minimum retirement age set by your employer' (report on line 1h); p. 30: 'You must include in your income any amounts that you received that you would have received in retirement had you not become disabled as a result of a terrorist attack.'
findings.fix: Reword the gate as 'For this person (you, or your spouse on a joint return) — was any of this paid because that person became disabled, under a plan that provides for disability retirement?'

findings.who: A contractor disabled in the World Trade Center cleanup who retired early on disability. The plan pays the normal retirement benefit instead of the reduced early benefit. The contractor thinks of the payments as an ordinary early-retirement pension.
findings.why_no: The contractor reads 'paid to you because you became disabled' as excluding a pension they would have received anyway at early-retirement age. Only the disability increment is attributable to the disability, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 30 Example: 'Until you turn age 62, you can exclude $500 of your monthly retirement benefit from income ... received on account of disability.'
findings.fix: Reword the gate as 'Was any of this paid, or paid at a higher amount or earlier date, because you or your spouse became disabled?' Ask the terrorist-attack question for every pension where either spouse is disabled.

locators: pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

findings.who: A filer took money out of a traditional IRA and put it back into the same IRA within 60 days, after an earlier IRA-to-IRA rollover in the prior 12 months.
findings.why_no: The gate reads 'put some into another retirement account'. A filer who redeposited into the same account can truthfully say no money went into another account. The gate then stays false, and the second-rollover question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: p590a (2025) p. 25: "You can make only one rollover from an IRA to another (or the same) IRA in any 1-year period regardless of the number of IRAs you own"
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you put any of this money back into a retirement account, including the same IRA it came from (within 60 days, or later under a waiver)?' and drop 'another' from the gate text.

findings.who: A filer received an IRA distribution in late December 2025 and redeposited it into an IRA in January 2026, within 60 days. An earlier IRA-to-IRA rollover falls in the 12 months before the December distribution.
findings.why_no: The filer reads the gate as asking what happened in the tax year, or with this year's money, and answers no because the redeposit happened in 2026. The gate turns false and the one-rollover limit is never tested.
findings.irs_text: p590a (2025) p. 25: "If you rolled over the distribution into a qualified plan (other than an IRA) or you make the rollover in 2026, attach a statement explaining what you did"; "The 1-year period begins on the date you receive the IRA distribution, not on the date you roll it over into an IRA"
findings.fix: Add to the gate's help: 'Count money you put back in 2026 (within 60 days of receiving it, or later under a waiver), even though you received it in 2025.'

findings.who: A joint return in which this Form 1099-R belongs to the spouse. The spouse had already rolled over a different IRA withdrawal within the prior 12 months, and the primary filer had none.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks whether 'you had also taken other money out of an IRA'. The person at the keyboard answers about their own IRAs, says no, and the spouse's second rollover passes without the refusal.
findings.irs_text: p590a (2025) p. 25: "The limit will apply by aggregating all of an individual's IRAs (whether traditional, Roth, or SIMPLE), effectively treating them as one IRA for purposes of the limit"
findings.fix: Name the IRA owner of this distribution in the question, for example 'Had [owner name] taken other money out of one of [his/her] own IRAs...'. Add to the help that only that person's IRAs count, not the spouse's.

locators: p. 25, Application of one-rollover-per-year limitation, "You can make only one rollover from an IRA to another (or the same) IRA in any 1-year period regardless of the number of IRAs you own"

p. 25, Application of one-rollover-per-year limitation, "You can make only one rollover from an IRA to another (or the same) IRA in any 1-year period regardless of the number of IRAs you own", "However, trustee-to-trustee transfers between IRAs aren’t limited and rollovers from traditional IRAs to Roth IRAs (conversions) aren’t limited"; p. 25, "The 1-year period begins on the date you receive the IRA distribution, not on the date you roll it over into an IRA"

findings.who: A filer started a series of substantially equal payments at 57 in 2022 and reached 59½ in 2025. In 2025 they took an extra withdrawal, which changes the series before the 5th anniversary of its first payment. The payer coded the 2025 Form 1099-R with code 7 (normal distribution) because the filer was over 59½.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from box 7. It is false because the code is 7, not 2, so the question about a series changed in 2025 is never asked.
findings.line: retirement.code2_partial_if_code2 (the refusal for recapture tax is missed)
findings.irs_text: p590b p. 26: "The recapture tax applies if you modify the series of payments ... before the later of these two dates: 1. The 5th anniversary of the date of the first distribution of the series; or 2. The date you reach age 59½." and "The recapture tax is imposed in the tax year in which the modification occurs."
findings.fix: Ask a separate per-person question for every return, whatever the box 7 code: 'Did you or your spouse start a series of substantially equal payments before 2025, and in 2025 change, stop, or add to it before age 59½ or within 5 years of its first payment?' Ask it once per person, not per Form 1099-R. A yes should lead to the refusal.

findings.who: An IRA owner under 59½ takes a series of substantially equal payments. The IRA custodian does not track the series and codes each Form 1099-R with code 1. In 2025 the owner took more than the series amount, so the series was changed.
findings.why_no: The box 7 code is 1, not 2. The gate is false, so the question about a changed series is never asked, even though the change triggers recapture of the tax on earlier years' payments.
findings.line: retirement.code2_partial_if_code2 (the refusal for recapture tax is missed)
findings.irs_text: p590b p. 26: "You may have to pay a recapture tax if you modify ... the annual amount distributed ... under the substantially equal periodic payment exception"; i5329 p. 5 lists the exception (No. 02) apart from the payer's code
findings.fix: Ask about a changed series apart from the code 2 gate, as above. Also ask it on the code 1 path, where the filer claims the series exception.

findings.who: A filer under 59½ stopped or skipped the 2025 payment from a series begun in 2023, so the account issued no 2025 Form 1099-R. Their other Forms 1099-R carry codes 7 or G.
findings.why_no: With no 2025 Form 1099-R from the series account, no document has code 2, so the gate never turns true. Stopping payments is a change of the series made in 2025.
findings.line: retirement.code2_partial_if_code2 (the refusal for recapture tax is missed)
findings.irs_text: p590b p. 26: "The recapture tax is imposed in the tax year in which the modification occurs." Of the payment changes, only a fully depleted account or a one-time switch to the RMD method is "not treated as a modification."
findings.fix: Ask the question about a changed series at the return level for each person, not only when a Form 1099-R with code 2 exists.

findings.who: A filer's Form 1099-R shows code 2 together with a second code in box 7, such as '2B' (designated Roth account) or '2K'. The code 2 exception covers only part of the money.
findings.why_no: If the helper 'Distribution code in box 7' turns the two codes into a value other than 'early_exception_2', the gate is false and the partial-exception question is skipped.
findings.irs_text: i5329 p. 5, Line 2: "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude."
findings.fix: Compute the gate as true whenever either box 7 code is 2, including the two-code combinations with 2.

locators: p. 5, Line 2, "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude."

p. 5, Line 2, "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude."; , "You may have to pay a recapture tax if you modify ... the annual amount distributed ... under the substantially equal periodic payment exception" and "The recapture tax is imposed in the tax year in which the modification occurs"

used.how: pages named by another document's citation

findings.who: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, whose Form 1099-R shows code 1, J or S in box 7, but who was already 59½ or older when they received the money. The payer coded the distribution as early by mistake.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as code = 'normal_7'. A code 1, J or S form fails it, so the age question is never asked and the age line is forced to false. The tool never learns the filer's age for exactly the codes where the IRS makes age decide the exclusion.
findings.line: retirement.under59_if_code7 (and the line 2 exclusion, exception 12, that depends on age at receipt)
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2, exception 12: "Distributions incorrectly indicated as early distributions by code 1, J, or S in box 7 of Form 1099-R. Include on line 2 the amount you received when you were age 59 1/2 or older."
findings.fix: Ask the age question whenever box 7 is code 1, J, S or 7, not only code 7. For codes 1, J and S, ask: 'Were you (or your spouse, for this form) age 59½ or older when you received any of this money? If so, how much did you receive on or after the date you reached 59½?' Feed the answer to line 2 as exception 12.

findings.who: A filer who turned 59½ during 2025 and received part of the distribution before that date and part after. The form shows code 1 (or J or S) because payments started early.
findings.why_no: The gate is false for code 1, so no age or timing question is asked. Even under code 7, the yes/no 'any of this money' cannot record the dollar split that exception 12 needs.
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2: "Include on line 2 the amount you received when you were age 59 1/2 or older."
findings.fix: For codes 1, J, S and 7, ask the date the person reached 59½ and the amount received on or after that date. Do not rely on a single yes/no about age.

findings.who: A filer whose box 7 holds a two-character code that includes 7 (for example 7D, 7K, 7M or B7). These mark a normal distribution with an annuity, IRA asset or plan-loan feature, or from a designated Roth account.
findings.why_no: If the helper maps only a bare '7' to 'normal_7', a combined code fails the gate. The age question is skipped, and an under-59½ recipient of a payment wrongly coded as normal is treated as not under 59½.
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2: "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude." Exceptions apply only to early distributions, so age at receipt decides whether the line 1 amount and line 2 exclusion exist at all.
findings.fix: Define the gate as 'box 7 contains code 7 alone or with any other code'. Or ask the age question for every Form 1099-R regardless of code.

locators: p. 5, Line 2, "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude."

findings.who: A filer whose Form 1099-R box 7 shows code 4 together with a second code, such as 4D, 4G, 4H, 4B, 4K or 48. Examples are a surviving spouse taking annuity payments from the decedent's plan (4D), or a beneficiary of a designated Roth account (4B).
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as box 7 code = 'death_4'. If the helper maps a two-character combination to another value, the gate is false even though code 4 is present. The question is then never asked, and a surviving spouse who has made the account her own never reaches the Yes that ends the interview.
findings.irs_text: i5329 p. 5, Line 2: "Distributions due to death (doesn't apply to modified endowment contracts)." The exception is for beneficiaries, so the refusal is needed whenever code 4 appears, alone or combined.
findings.fix: Compute the gate as 'box 7 contains code 4' (any combination that includes 4), not as equality with a single enumerated value.

findings.who: A surviving spouse who rolled the deceased spouse's IRA, or a plan payout, into her own existing IRA, or retitled it in her own name. A later distribution from that account still came with code 4.
findings.why_no: The question lists three ways of making the IRA your own: choosing to, putting money into it, and skipping a required minimum distribution. She did none of these to 'the IRA' as she understands it, since she moved the money into a different IRA. She reads the list as complete and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5329 p. 5, Line 2: "Distributions due to death". Once the spouse treats or rolls the IRA as her own, she is no longer a beneficiary and the death exception does not apply.
findings.fix: Add 'or rolled it over into your own IRA or retitled it in your name' and say that the list is not exhaustive: 'in any way, including ...'.

findings.who: A surviving spouse who received a code-4 distribution from her late husband's 401(k) or 403(b), after earlier electing to treat the account as her own or rolling it to her own plan or IRA.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether she has 'made the IRA your own'. Her account is not an IRA, so she answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5329 p. 5, Line 2: "Distributions due to death (doesn't apply to modified endowment contracts)." The exception depends on receiving the money as a beneficiary, whatever the type of plan.
findings.fix: Say 'made the IRA or retirement plan account your own (including by rolling it into your own account)'.

locators: pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method
p. 5, Line 2, "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude."

findings.who: A filer age 70 1/2 or older whose employer funded a SEP-IRA or SIMPLE IRA had the trustee send part of it directly to a charity. Or a filer made a one-time HSA funding distribution from that account.
findings.why_no: The account came through the employer and is called a 'SEP plan' or 'SIMPLE plan', so the filer picks 'plan' as the kind of account. The IRA branch is then false, and the charity/HSA question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 26: 'an IRA includes a traditional IRA (which includes a traditional IRA that receives contributions from a simplified employee pension (SEP) arrangement)... and a SIMPLE IRA'; p. 27 Exception 3: 'If all or part of the distribution is a qualified charitable distribution (QCD)...'
findings.fix: Classify the account from Form 1099-R box 7: an X in the 'IRA/SEP/SIMPLE' checkbox means IRA. Or say in the helper's options: 'SEP-IRA and SIMPLE IRA accounts from an employer count as IRAs, not plans.'

findings.who: A filer whose employer SIMPLE IRA or SEP-IRA paid back an excess contribution, or a 2024 or 2025 contribution, in 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer reads the employer arrangement as a 'plan', so the IRA branch is false and the returned-contribution question, which leads to a refusal, is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: '4. You had a 2024 or 2025 IRA contribution returned to you... 5. You made excess contributions to your IRA for an earlier year and had them returned to you in 2025.'
findings.fix: Use the box 7 IRA/SEP/SIMPLE checkbox to decide the branch, not the filer's word 'plan'.

findings.who: A retiree receiving one of these on a Form 1099-R or CSA 1099-R: military retired pay, a federal civil service annuity, a state or local government pension, or a 403(b) annuity contract with an insurer. Or a beneficiary receiving a deceased parent's pension.
findings.why_no: The filer does not think of a government pension, military retired pay or an insurance annuity as a 'plan'. They choose another kind of account, and because the gate is '≠ plan', any non-plan choice is treated as an IRA. The plan questions are then skipped.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 28: 'Fully taxable pensions and annuities also include military retirement pay'; 'An eligible retirement plan is a governmental plan that is a qualified trust or a section 403(a), 403(b), or 457(b) plan'; p. 30 Cost: 'Your net investment may be shown in box 9b of Form 1099-R.'
findings.fix: Compute the gate as 'kind = IRA' (an IRA/SEP/SIMPLE checkbox on Form 1099-R), not '≠ plan'. Label the plan option broadly: 'pension, annuity, 401(k)/403(b)/457(b), military or civil service retired pay, or any other employer or government plan'.

findings.who: A Form 1099-R box 7 shows code 8, P or G, and box 2b 'Total distribution' is checked, so the filer reads the form as a refund or a rollover. Or a 401(k) loan was offset on separation, with code M or L, and no cash was paid out.
findings.why_no: No money arrived and the form looks unlike a pension payment, so the filer chooses a non-plan or 'other' option. The '≠ plan' gate then routes the form to the IRA branch.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 28: 'Pension and annuity payments include distributions from 401(k), 403(b), and governmental 457(b) plans'; p. 30 Rollovers: 'Use lines 5a and 5b to report a rollover, including a direct rollover, from one qualified employer's plan to another or to an IRA.'
findings.fix: Decide the branch from the 1099-R itself (the IRA/SEP/SIMPLE checkbox), with no fallback that treats unrecognized kinds as IRA.

findings.who: On a joint return, the spouse owns the IRA or the plan, and the 'kind of account' helper is asked in the second person.
findings.why_no: The filer answers about their own accounts ('I have a 401(k)'), not about the spouse's account on this 1099-R, and so picks the wrong branch.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27: 'If you file a joint return, the same rules apply to your spouse'; p. 30: 'If you or the plan participant was born before January 2, 1936, you could pay less tax on the distribution.'
findings.fix: Word the helper as 'What kind of account paid out the money on this Form 1099-R (yours or your spouse's)?'

locators: p. 26, Lines 4a and 4b, IRA Distributions
pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

findings.who: An owner took a 2025 distribution from a SEP IRA or a SIMPLE IRA. The same owner has a separate traditional IRA funded with nondeductible contributions, and earlier returns included Form 8606.
findings.why_no: The gate's label reads 'A traditional, SEP or SIMPLE IRA', but it is computed only as kind = 'traditional_ira'. If the 'Kind of account' helper lists SEP IRA or SIMPLE IRA as separate choices, this filer truthfully picks one of those, and the gate comes out false.
findings.line: retirement.ira_basis_if_trad (and the refusal a Yes triggers)
findings.irs_text: i8606 (2025) p. 2, Purpose of Form: 'Distributions from traditional IRAs, if you have a basis in these IRAs'. Definitions list 'SEP IRAs: Traditional and Roth' and 'SIMPLE IRAs: Traditional and Roth'. i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2(1): 'a distribution from an IRA (other than a Roth IRA) and you made nondeductible contributions to any of your traditional IRAs'.
findings.fix: Compute the gate as kind in {traditional_ira, sep_ira, simple_ira, inherited_traditional_ira}. Better: gate on Form 1099-R box 'IRA/SEP/SIMPLE' being checked and the account not being a Roth, and ask the basis question about all of the owner's traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs together.

findings.who: A beneficiary received a 2025 distribution from a traditional IRA inherited from a parent. The parent had made nondeductible contributions and filed Form 8606.
findings.why_no: If the helper offers 'inherited IRA' or 'beneficiary distribution' as its own kind, the filer picks it instead of 'traditional IRA', and the gate is false. The gated question even names inherited basis, but it is never asked.
findings.line: retirement.ira_basis_if_trad (and the refusal a Yes triggers)
findings.irs_text: i8606 (2025) p. 2, Who Must File: 'You received a distribution from an inherited traditional IRA that has a basis'.
findings.fix: Treat an inherited traditional, SEP or SIMPLE IRA as traditional for this gate. Alternatively, ask 'Did this come from an IRA that is not a Roth IRA, including one you inherited?'

findings.who: An owner's traditional IRA is an individual retirement annuity bought from a life insurance company. The insurer's Form 1099-R reports annuity payments. The owner made nondeductible contributions in past years.
findings.why_no: The filer sees an insurance company as the issuer and 'annuity' payments, so they classify the account as an annuity or pension rather than a traditional IRA, and the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: i8606 (2025) p. 2: 'An IRA is an individual retirement account or an individual retirement annuity... You can open an individual retirement annuity by purchasing an annuity contract or an endowment contract from a life insurance company.'
findings.fix: Classify the account from the checked 'IRA/SEP/SIMPLE' box on Form 1099-R, not from the filer's description. Help text should say that an IRA held as an annuity with an insurer counts as a traditional IRA.

findings.who: On a joint return, one spouse has several 2025 Forms 1099-R: one from a 401(k) and one from a traditional IRA that holds basis. Alternatively, the spouse with the basis is not the spouse whose account the helper describes.
findings.why_no: The gate depends on 'the distribution' in the singular. If the kind is captured once per person, or once per return, rather than once per Form 1099-R, the filer answers for the 401(k) distribution. The traditional-IRA basis question is then never asked for the person who owns that IRA.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 27: 'If you (or your spouse if filing jointly) received more than one distribution, figure the taxable amount of each distribution'. i8606 p. 2: 'You received distributions from a traditional IRA in 2025 and your basis in these IRAs is more than zero'.
findings.fix: Evaluate the gate per owner as 'any 2025 distribution of this person came from a non-Roth IRA', and ask the basis question once for each such owner.

findings.who: An employee received a distribution from a deemed traditional IRA (section 408(q)) held inside an employer's 401(k) or 457(b) plan, funded with nondeductible contributions.
findings.why_no: The plan administrator issues the form, and the account sits in the work plan, so the filer picks 'employer plan' as the kind.
findings.irs_text: i8606 (2025) p. 2, Definitions: '• Deemed IRAs. • Traditional IRAs.'; Purpose of Form: 'Distributions from traditional IRAs, if you have a basis in these IRAs'.
findings.fix: Rely on the 1099-R 'IRA/SEP/SIMPLE' box. Help text for the kind helper should say that an IRA held within an employer plan counts as an IRA.

findings.who: In 2025, under a divorce agreement, a spouse transferred part of a traditional IRA that held basis to the other spouse, which changed each spouse's basis. The receiving spouse also took a distribution, classified under a different kind such as a SIMPLE IRA or an inherited IRA.
findings.why_no: The gate is false because of the account kind, so the question that names 'basis that came with an IRA from a spouse in a divorce' is never reached. The refusal for a Form 8606 situation is missed.
findings.irs_text: i8606 (2025) p. 2, Who Must File: 'You or your spouse transferred all or part of their traditional IRA in 2025 to the other spouse under a divorce or separation agreement where the transfer resulted in a change in the basis'. p. 9, Line 2: 'Incident to divorce, you transferred or received part or all of a traditional IRA'.
findings.fix: Ask a separate, ungated per-person question about any 2025 transfer of a traditional IRA incident to divorce, and refuse when the answer is Yes.

locators: pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

p. 2, Who Must File, "You received distributions from a traditional IRA in 2025 and your basis in these IRAs is more than zero", "You or your spouse transferred all or part of their traditional IRA in 2025 to the other spouse under a divorce or separation agreement where the transfer resulted in a change in the basis", and "You received a distribution from an inherited traditional IRA that has a basis"; p. 9, Line 2, "You rolled over any nontaxable portion of your qualified retirement plan to a traditional IRA"

findings.who: A surviving spouse or other beneficiary receives a continuing survivor annuity or guaranteed-period payments after a retiree died. The payer (some state or municipal systems, or a payer that kept the retiree's account coding) reports it on Form 1099-R with box 7 code 7, not code 4.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from box 7 code 4 rather than from the fact that the payee is a beneficiary of someone who died. The filer enters code 7 from the form, so the gate is false and none of the beneficiary questions are asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30: "If you are the survivor of a retiree, use the retiree's age on their annuity starting date... If you are the beneficiary of an employee who died, see Pub. 575. If there is more than one beneficiary, see Pub. 575 or Pub. 721 to figure each beneficiary's taxable amount."
findings.fix: Gate on a fact question asked of every non-IRA Form 1099-R: "Are you receiving this because someone else (the worker or retiree) died, whatever code is in box 7?" Treat a yes, or code 4, as the death branch.

findings.who: A widow is still receiving a survivor annuity in 2025 from a worker who died before August 21, 1996. After decades of payments, the payer codes the Form 1099-R as a normal distribution (code 7).
findings.why_no: The computed gate needs code 4, so the death benefit exclusion question is never asked. The tool also never refuses, even though the worksheet requires the exclusion to be added to cost.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 29, Simplified Method Worksheet: "If you are the beneficiary of a deceased employee or former employee who died before August 21, 1996, include any death benefit exclusion that you are entitled to (up to $5,000) in the amount entered on line 2 below."
findings.fix: Ask whether the payments are made because of someone's death independently of the box 7 code, and route a yes to the death-benefit-exclusion question.

findings.who: A nonspouse beneficiary's Form 1099-R shows box 7 as a two-character code that includes 4, such as 4D, 4B (designated Roth), 4H, 4K or 4G. They rolled part of the distribution over within 60 days.
findings.why_no: If the helper "Code 4 (death)" matches only the exact entry "4", a combined code makes the gate false. The nonspouse-rollover refusal and the beneficiary questions are then skipped.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 24: "A distribution paid to a beneficiary other than the employee's surviving spouse is generally not an eligible rollover distribution... The distribution must be a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to your traditional or Roth IRA that was set up to receive the distribution."
findings.fix: Define the helper so it is true whenever either character of box 7 is 4.

findings.who: A survivor receives federal civil service survivor benefits on OPM's CSA/CSF 1099-R, or railroad survivor benefits on Form RRB-1099-R. These forms do not follow the standard code-4 convention.
findings.why_no: The gate keys on the standard Form 1099-R box 7 code 4, which these forms may not carry. The beneficiary questions are reached only through that code.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30: "If there is more than one beneficiary, see Pub. 575 or Pub. 721 to figure each beneficiary's taxable amount."; i1040gi p. 28: "If you received a Form RRB-1099-R, see Pub. 575 to find out how to report your benefits."
findings.fix: Ask the death or beneficiary fact for every pension or annuity source, including OPM and RRB forms, or refuse those survivor forms outright.

findings.who: A nonspouse beneficiary's payer coded the distribution 4 correctly, but the filer received it as cash and redeposited part of it into their own IRA within 60 days.
findings.why_no: The line's label says "of which some went into another retirement account". If the rollover sub-condition is computed only from a direct-rollover code (G) or from the filer's own rollover entry, a filer who does not see a cash redeposit as a rollover goes unasked.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 24: "Rollovers by nonspouse beneficiary... The distribution must be a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to your traditional or Roth IRA that was set up to receive the distribution."
findings.fix: Ask any code-4 plan beneficiary: "Did you put any of this money into an IRA or another plan, by any means, including a deposit within 60 days?"

locators: pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

p. 5, Inherited from someone other than spouse, "you can't roll over any amounts into or out of the inherited IRA"; , Rollovers by nonspouse beneficiary, "The distribution must be a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to your traditional or Roth IRA that was set up to receive the distribution."

p. 5, Inherited from someone other than spouse, "you can't roll over any amounts into or out of the inherited IRA. However, you can make a trustee-to-trustee transfer"; , Rollovers by nonspouse beneficiary, "The distribution must be a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to your traditional or Roth IRA that was set up to receive the distribution."

used.how: pages named by another document's citation

findings.who: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, converted a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA at the same custodian. The custodian issued a 2025 Form 1099-R with code 2 or 7, not G, and the filer thinks of it as 'converting my IRA', not moving money to a new account.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'went into another retirement account' and gives a direct rollover as its example. An in-place conversion does not feel like putting money into another account, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: "However, a rollover to a Roth IRA or a designated Roth account is generally not a tax-free distribution." (i1040gi 2025 p. 30, Rollovers); "3. You converted part or all of a traditional IRA or traditional SIMPLE IRA to a Roth IRA in 2025." (i1040gi 2025 p. 27, Exception 2)
findings.fix: Ask the Roth question outside the gate, or broaden the gate: 'Did you (or your spouse) roll over, convert, or move any of this money into any retirement account, including a Roth IRA, a Roth account in the same plan, or back into the same account?'

findings.who: A filer took money out of an IRA (traditional or Roth) and redeposited it into the same IRA within 60 days, a 60-day rollover with no new account. This includes a filer whose IRS-levied IRA money was returned and put back into the original IRA.
findings.why_no: The gate's words 'another retirement account' exclude putting the money back into the account it came from, so the filer truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: "Exception 1. Enter the total distribution on line 4a if you rolled over part or all of the distribution from one: • Roth IRA to another Roth IRA, or • IRA (other than a Roth IRA) to a qualified plan or another IRA ... Generally, a rollover must be made within 60 days after the day you received the distribution." (i1040gi 2025 p. 27)
findings.fix: Drop 'another' and say 'any retirement account, including the same account it came from'. Ask the levy question whenever the Form 1099-R is from an IRA or plan, not only after a yes to the gate.

findings.who: A plan paid out employer stock or other shares in kind. The filer moved some of the shares into an IRA and kept or sold the rest, and no cash changed hands.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'some of the money' went into another retirement account. A filer who received and moved only shares reads 'money' as cash and answers no.
findings.irs_text: "Generally, a rollover is a tax-free distribution of cash or other assets from one retirement plan that is contributed to another plan within 60 days ... See Pub. 575 for more details on rollovers, including ... partial rollovers of property" (i1040gi 2025 p. 30, Rollovers)
findings.fix: Word the gate: 'Did any of this distribution (cash, shares, or other property) go into a retirement account, or did you sell property from it and put the proceeds into one?'

findings.who: A filer received a distribution in late December 2025 and completed the 60-day rollover in January or February 2026.
findings.why_no: The filer reads the question as being about 2025 events and does not count a deposit made in 2026.
findings.irs_text: "If you rolled over the distribution into a qualified plan or you made the rollover in 2026, include a statement explaining what you did." (i1040gi 2025 p. 27)
findings.fix: Add to the gate's help: 'Count a rollover made within 60 days even if it happened in 2026.'

locators: pp. 27-30, lines 4a-5b: Exceptions 2-4, Lump-Sum Distributions, Insurance Premiums for Retired Public Safety Officers, Simplified Method

findings.who: A filer, or the spouse on a joint return, leaves a job in 2025 with an outstanding 401(k) loan. The plan offsets the account balance to repay the loan, so no cash is paid out. Before the extended due date, the filer deposits an equal amount of their own savings into a traditional IRA to complete a qualified plan loan offset rollover.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'any of this money' went into a retirement account. The offset amount never reached the filer, and the dollars deposited came from savings, so 'this money' truthfully did not go anywhere. The gated question's '60 days' wording and 'A later deposit counts only under an IRS waiver' also tell the filer that a deposit months later cannot count.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 23: 'if you have a qualified plan loan offset, you will have until the due date (including extensions) for your tax return for the tax year in which the offset occurs to complete your rollover.'
findings.fix: Make the gate turn on an amount the filer deposited, not on the same money: 'Did you put any amount into a retirement plan or IRA as a rollover of this distribution, including a deposit of your own funds to replace a plan loan offset, withheld tax, or money you spent?' In the gated question, allow the due date (with extensions) for a qualified plan loan offset.

findings.who: A filer takes a qualified birth or adoption distribution of up to $5,000 from a 401(k) or IRA in 2025 and repays part of it to an eligible plan later in 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of this as 'repaying' the withdrawal, not as a rollover or conversion. The help names only Roth moves and the cancelled first-home purchase as special cases. The gated question's '60 days' and 'A later deposit counts only under an IRS waiver' tell the filer that a repayment months later does not count.
findings.irs_text: p590b p. 28: 'you can make one or more contributions to an eligible retirement plan during the 3-year period beginning on the day after the date the distribution was received... Any contribution made to the eligible retirement plan as a repayment of a qualified birth or adoption distribution may be eligible for tax-free rollover treatment.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate help: 'Repaying a birth or adoption withdrawal (within 3 years) or an emergency or disaster withdrawal counts as putting money back.' In the gated question, list the 3-year repayment window beside the 60-day and 120-day windows.

findings.who: A filer receives a distribution of stock from an employer plan, or shares in kind from an IRA. The filer either sells the stock and deposits the cash proceeds in a traditional IRA within 60 days, or transfers the same shares into an IRA.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'this money', and the help says 'If all of it stayed with you'. The distribution was stock, not money. If the stock was sold, the cash deposited is sale proceeds, which the filer may treat as a separate event.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 23: 'To roll over an eligible rollover distribution of property, you must either roll over the actual property distributed or sell it and roll over the proceeds.'; p590a p. 25: 'your rollover is tax free only if the property you contribute is the same property that was distributed to you.'
findings.fix: Replace 'this money' with 'this distribution (cash, stock, or other property)', and add to the help: 'Selling distributed property and depositing the proceeds also counts.'

findings.who: A filer receives an IRA or plan distribution in mid-December 2025 and completes the 60-day rollover in January 2026.
findings.why_no: The whole return is about 2025, so the filer may read the gate as asking about deposits made in 2025 and answer no, because the deposit was made in 2026.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 1: 'If you rolled over the distribution into a qualified plan or you made the rollover in 2026, include a statement explaining what you did.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count a deposit made in 2026 if it was within 60 days (or the allowed extension) of a 2025 distribution.'

findings.who: A surviving spouse or a non-spouse designated beneficiary has a deceased employee's plan balance moved by direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into an IRA set up to receive it.
findings.why_no: The words 'again' and 'rollover' suggest the filer's own money returning to an account. A beneficiary may see the transfer as setting up an inheritance, not as a rollover of 'this money'.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 24: 'The distribution must be a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to your traditional or Roth IRA that was set up to receive the distribution. The transfer will be treated as an eligible rollover distribution'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'A direct transfer from the plan to an IRA, including an inherited IRA set up to receive a beneficiary's share, counts.'

This contribution is treated as a rollover contribution to the IRA."

findings.who: A filer who reached age 59½ partway through 2025 and received code 7 payments both before and after that date, such as monthly payments starting in January when they reach 59½ in August. Some of the money may not be from a section 457 plan, or may be rollover money inside the 457 plan.
findings.why_no: They are 59½ or older now and at year end, so they answer by their age when filing or on December 31 rather than on each payment date. They may also not know which date makes them 59½, or they may read 'any of this money' as 'this distribution' and think of the most recent payments.
findings.line: retirement.sec457_if_under59 (forced false; the refusal for a code 7 distribution before age 59½ that is not from a section 457 plan is skipped, so the 10% additional tax on the early portion goes unreported)
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2: 'Distributions from a section 457 plan, which aren't from a rollover from a qualified retirement plan.' Exception 12: 'Include on line 2 the amount you received when you were age 59 1/2 or older.' Line 2 depends on age at each receipt.
findings.fix: Ask for the date of birth and the payment dates, or the total paid before the 59½ date, and compute the gate. Or reword: 'Was any payment in this 2025 total made before the date you turned 59½ (6 months after your 59th birthday)? Count each payment separately, even if you are older than 59½ now.'

findings.who: Joint filers where one spouse is 62 and the other is 52. The younger spouse received a code 7 Form 1099-R, for example from a government 457(b) plan that includes rollover money, or a code 7 issued in error.
findings.why_no: The gate asks 'Were you under age 59½…', but the gated question names 'this person (you, or your spouse on a joint return)'. The older spouse filling in the return reads 'you' as themselves and answers no.
findings.line: retirement.sec457_if_under59 (forced false; the refusal or the exception 12 handling for the spouse's early distribution is skipped)
findings.irs_text: i5329 (2025) p. 5, Line 2: 'Distributions from a section 457 plan, which aren't from a rollover from a qualified retirement plan.' The exception and the additional tax depend on the age of the person who received the money.
findings.fix: Name the recipient in the gate: 'Was [name on this Form 1099-R] under age 59½ on the date any of this money was paid?' Better, compute the gate from that person's date of birth.

locators: p. 5, Line 2, "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude."
